Religion. A social system built on shared beliefs about the sacred, organized rituals, and moral frameworks that give meaning to human existence.

Religions vary enormously across cultures, time periods, and expressions, from monotheistic faiths to animistic traditions to philosophical systems, but all share the function of addressing ultimate questions of meaning, morality, and human purpose. Religions typically include a supernatural component with belief in gods, spirits, or transcendent forces, and a social institutional structure that binds communities together through shared meaning.

Ritual practice is usually central to religion. Worship, prayer, sacrifice, and initiation ceremonies transmit and reinforce religious identity across generations and mark passages in individual lives. Anthropologist Clifford Geertz defined religion as a system of symbols that establishes powerful moods and motivations among believers, functioning as both cognitive framework and emotional experience. Religion functions to address existential anxiety, enforce social norms, validate authority structures, create in-group cohesion, and provide frameworks for interpreting suffering and injustice.

Magic and religion are often conflated but analytically distinct. Magic assumes manipulation of impersonal forces through technical procedure, while religion assumes relationship with personal beings such as gods or ancestors through supplication and trust. Secularization theory posits that modernization erodes religious belief, though global data shows religion remains influential even in developed nations and that religious revivals occur cyclically.

Major world religions including Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Judaism number over two billion adherents, while millions follow indigenous religions, syncretistic traditions, and new religious movements. The relationship between religion and other domains such as science, politics, and law remains contested. Some societies mandate separation of church and state, while others interweave religious authority with governmental power.
